title: Connectivity Diagnosis
summary: Distinguish device, Wi-Fi/LAN, ISP, service-availability and application-layer problems before prescribing a fix.

stages.title: What are we diagnosing?
stages.body: A connection problem can occur at several layers: device → local Wi-Fi/LAN → school/library network → ISP/backhaul → remote service. 'Internet is down' is not precise enough to choose an intervention.
actions: Check whether one device or many are affected.
Compare Wi-Fi and wired/mobile connectivity if available.
Record time, location and affected service without recording student PII.

stages.title: Run a five-layer check
stages.body: Start local and move outward. This prevents expensive infrastructure proposals when the actual fault is a device, DNS, captive portal or local access point.
actions: Device: airplane mode, adapter state, IP address.
LAN/Wi-Fi: signal, gateway reachability, another device.
Internet: known public site or speed/latency check.
Service: check whether only one platform fails.
Evidence: compare FCC/BDO availability with observed performance; availability is not adoption or experienced quality.

stages.title: Measure the right variables
stages.body: Latency, jitter, packet loss, upload capacity, contention, DNS resolution and firewall policy can matter as much as headline download speed for video instruction, telehealth and WebRTC.
actions: Collect aggregate tests at multiple times.
Separate advertised availability from measured performance.
Document network policy constraints that could block WebRTC or WebGPU asset downloads.

stages.title: Design an evidence-grade diagnostic
stages.body: Use repeatable measurement windows, device/network metadata, privacy-safe aggregation, topology diagrams and change logs. If proposing infrastructure, connect the diagnosed bottleneck to the intervention and define post-change acceptance tests.
actions: Create baseline/after metrics.
Keep raw identifiers out of shared rooms.
Record source, date, geography, method and uncertainty.

title: Trystero / WebRTC Multiplayer
summary: Understand decentralized discovery, direct peer traffic, room IDs, optional passwords, snapshots and TURN fallback.

stages.title: How the room works
stages.body: Trystero uses a discovery strategy to help browsers exchange WebRTC connection information. After peers connect, application data travels directly peer-to-peer rather than through a central application database.
actions: Use the same room ID and discovery strategy on participating devices.
Use a shared password when a room should not rely only on room/app identifiers for SDP encryption.

stages.title: Choose a strategy
stages.body: This build pins Trystero 0.25.3 and exposes Nostr, MQTT, BitTorrent and IPFS discovery. Nostr is the default; Trystero currently recommends the decentralized alternatives in roughly MQTT, BitTorrent, IPFS order after Nostr for robustness.
actions: Start with Nostr.
If discovery is unreliable, try MQTT, then BitTorrent, then IPFS.
Keep strategy identical among peers joining the same session.

stages.title: State synchronization
stages.body: Room actions use the 0.25.x object API. A joining peer requests a snapshot from an existing peer; timestamped shared records merge locally, while deletion tombstones prevent old snapshots from resurrecting deleted board items.
actions: Inspect peer count and snapshot status.
Export JSON backups for durable human-controlled history.
Treat peer IDs as ephemeral technical identifiers, not verified identities.

stages.title: NAT traversal and TURN
stages.body: STUN/direct WebRTC works across many networks, but not all NAT/firewall combinations. TURN is a relay fallback for pairs that cannot establish a direct connection; it is not hidden infrastructure in this build.
actions: Diagnose failures across different networks.
Add an organization-controlled TURN configuration only when needed.
For institutional deployment add SSO/admission controls separately from transport encryption.

title: Texas Broadband Project Status
summary: Read BEAD, BOOT, FCC and Texas mapping status without confusing awards, construction and actual service availability.

stages.title: Four different statuses
stages.body: A location can be mapped as unserved/underserved, included in an award, under construction, or actually served. Those are different states and should not be collapsed into one 'broadband available' flag.
actions: Open the Texas BDO maps and BEAD award map.
Record the map/data date before using it in an education plan.

stages.title: Use current Texas program context
stages.body: Texas' BEAD final proposal was approved December 4, 2025. The BDO reports 22 selected applicants, more than 240,000 broadband-serviceable locations and more than 2,700 community anchor institutions, with construction expected to begin as soon as summer 2026. BOOT I reports $10.4 million awarded for 1,468 residential locations, 77 businesses and 15 community anchor institutions; BOOT I projects are due by December 31, 2026.
actions: Check the BEAD award map for project/coverage status.
Check the BOOT I awardee status file for project completion.
Do not infer household adoption from infrastructure awards.

stages.title: Connect broadband status to education
stages.body: For a school or library, distinguish middle-mile/backhaul, last-mile availability, campus WAN, internal Wi-Fi, device access and affordability. E-rate can address eligible school/library connectivity components while BEAD/BOOT address different infrastructure scopes.
actions: Map school/library anchor institutions to project areas.
Separate facility connectivity from student home connectivity.
Track E-rate funding-year deadlines independently of construction programs.

stages.title: Build a project-status ledger
stages.body: Use a record per project/area with program, awardee, award date, agreement status, construction state, completion state, source URL, retrieval date and confidence. Never infer construction completion from an award announcement.
actions: Refresh BDO/FCC sources on a schedule.
Retain superseded records for provenance.
Flag conflicting map/project evidence for human review.

title: Mapping & Challenge Workflows
summary: Understand FCC/Texas broadband maps, challenge mechanisms and the difference between mapped availability and lived connectivity.

stages.title: Maps are evidence, not reality itself
stages.body: Broadband maps are administrative/technical representations assembled from provider and location data. They are useful, but individual locations can be wrong or outdated.
actions: Check the FCC National Broadband Map by address when appropriate.
Use aggregate rather than student-identifying location data in shared planning rooms.

stages.title: Classify the mismatch
stages.body: The Texas BDO points users to FCC availability, location and bulk challenge processes. A challenge should match the type of error instead of simply asserting the map is wrong.
actions: Identify availability vs location/fabric issue.
Collect the evidence required by the official process.
Check whether a program-specific challenge window is still open; the 2025 BEAD application challenge window is historical.

stages.title: Triangulate datasets
stages.body: Combine BDO/FCC availability, ACS household subscription, school/library network evidence and measured performance. These datasets answer different questions and should not be merged without preserving definitions.
actions: Attach data dictionary/definition to each layer.
Record geography and reference year.
Do not substitute subscription data for network availability.

stages.title: Spatial evidence governance
stages.body: Use reproducible geospatial joins, stable location identifiers where legally permitted, versioned source snapshots and explicit uncertainty. Protect household/student privacy when converting address-level evidence into school-planning layers.
actions: Aggregate sensitive records before collaboration.
Version geospatial layers.
Document transformation steps and exclusions.

title: Multidisciplinary Project Design
summary: Design interventions around dependencies and accountable handoffs rather than a single-domain solution list.

stages.title: Start with a capacity problem
stages.body: Define the measurable education problem first: for example, specialist-teacher access, apprenticeship transport or family broadband—not 'fix education.'
actions: Write one observable problem statement.
Name the affected population without exposing PII.
Choose one baseline measure.

stages.title: Map dependencies and owners
stages.body: Ask which domains can block or enable the outcome: staffing, housing, mobility, broadband, health, food, energy, water, employer/college capacity or library access.
actions: Assign a disciplinary owner to each dependency.
Create shared evidence and decision records.
Define a 30/60/90-day pilot.

stages.title: Use interfaces, not silos
stages.body: Each discipline should provide inputs, constraints, decisions and measurable outputs. A cross-domain project fails when responsibilities are implicit and no handoff has an owner.
actions: Add dependencies to the shared board.
Record decision rationale and evidence class.
Set stop/adjust criteria before scaling.

stages.title: Govern the system of systems
stages.body: Use a dependency graph, RACI-like accountability, provenance ledger, conflict-resolution process and outcome hierarchy. Measure both primary educational outcomes and externalities such as commute burden or infrastructure utilization.
actions: Define governance cadence.
Separate measured outcomes from modeled effects.
Publish a privacy-safe implementation log.

title: Telehealth & Learning Access
summary: Treat telehealth as a privacy-sensitive service dependency that can support families and staff without turning schools into health-data repositories.

stages.title: Where education intersects
stages.body: Health access can affect attendance and family/staff capacity, while libraries can provide private broadband-enabled spaces. The education system should coordinate access without collecting unnecessary clinical data.
actions: Map privacy-safe referral/access resources.
Do not record diagnoses in shared education rooms.

stages.title: Design an access pathway
stages.body: Identify an appropriate provider/service, private location, reliable connectivity, scheduling/transport constraints and consent/confidentiality requirements. Texas HHS program guidance emphasizes consent, confidentiality, quality and supervision for telemedicine where applicable.
actions: Use organization-approved telehealth procedures.
Verify current provider/payer/legal requirements.
Consider library privacy rooms where locally available and appropriate.

stages.title: Network quality matters
stages.body: Telehealth is sensitive to latency, jitter, packet loss, audio/video quality and privacy. A nominal broadband-availability flag is insufficient to demonstrate service readiness.
actions: Test the actual room/network.
Ensure acoustic/visual privacy.
Define failure/escalation path when connectivity drops.

stages.title: Govern cross-sector data boundaries
stages.body: Minimize information exchange between education and health organizations. Use referrals/status indicators rather than clinical details; define consent, retention, authorized access and incident handling before integrating systems.
actions: Create a data-flow diagram.
Classify protected/sensitive fields.
Run privacy/security review before production integration.

title: Emergency Communications for Learning Continuity
summary: Plan redundant, role-aware communications for closures, outages and continuity without relying on a single platform.

stages.title: Assume one channel can fail
stages.body: Power, cellular service, broadband, a vendor platform or a campus network can fail independently. Continuity plans need more than one way to communicate.
actions: List primary and backup channels.
Define who is authorized to issue official messages.
Keep emergency instructions available offline where possible.

stages.title: Build the communications ladder
stages.body: Use district emergency procedures first, then map redundant channels such as SMS/voice, web/PWA, radio/partner networks and physical/community anchor points where appropriate.
actions: Assign message owner and backup.
Prewrite accessible multilingual templates.
Test contact trees and offline materials.

stages.title: Separate coordination from public alerting
stages.body: A P2P room can support team coordination when peers can connect, but it is not a replacement for official mass-notification or public-safety systems. WebRTC itself may fail on restricted networks.
actions: Use P2P only as an additional coordination layer.
Document when to switch to approved emergency channels.
Treat TURN as optional transport resilience, not an emergency authority system.

stages.title: Exercise degraded modes
stages.body: Run tabletop and technical exercises that remove one dependency at a time: internet, power, cellular, DNS, identity provider or building access. Measure notification latency, reach and recovery.
actions: Record gaps and corrective actions.
Maintain offline contact/procedure artifacts securely.
Review accessibility and language access in exercises.

title: WebLLM Local AI
summary: Use browser-local inference as an optional planning aid while preserving verification, privacy and device capability boundaries.

stages.title: What happens locally?
stages.body: After the WebLLM library/model are downloaded, inference can run in the browser with WebGPU rather than sending prompts to a remote model API. This build runs heavy inference in a dedicated Web Worker so the interface remains responsive.
actions: Check WebGPU support.
Load a small model first.
Never place student-identifying records in prompts.

stages.title: Use it as a planning assistant
stages.body: Ask for project structures, evidence questions or cross-domain checklists. Treat generated content as unverified until supported by authoritative/local evidence.
actions: Ask the model to label facts vs assumptions.
Cross-check mutable Texas facts in the Evidence module.
Use the deterministic fallback if no model is available.

stages.title: Caching and performance
stages.body: First-run model downloads can be large. Browser storage, GPU memory and device thermals determine what is practical. A PWA being offline-ready does not automatically mean an uncached model is available offline.
actions: Track model download/caching status.
Choose smaller quantized models on constrained devices.
Do not promise offline AI until the exact model has loaded successfully before disconnecting.

stages.title: Worker architecture and governance
stages.body: The main page creates a WebWorkerMLCEngine client while a dedicated module worker hosts WebWorkerMLCEngineHandler. Keep model output outside automated high-stakes student/teacher decisions and retain human verification checkpoints.
actions: Pin/test WebLLM versions for production.
Define prompt/data policy.
Measure latency/memory before district-scale rollout.

title: PWA & Offline Architecture
summary: Know exactly what the service worker caches, what remains local and what still requires the network.

stages.title: Offline is not all-or-nothing
stages.body: The app shell, bundled evidence/guides and local IndexedDB records can work after successful caching. Live sources, first-time external libraries, Trystero discovery and uncached AI models still need connectivity.
actions: Load the site once over HTTPS.
Confirm service-worker readiness.
Export a JSON backup before major changes.

stages.title: Classify features
stages.body: Label each feature as bundled/offline, cached-after-use or live-only. This avoids misleading users during outages.
actions: Bundled: core UI, guides, evidence registry.
Local: projects, portfolio, room cache.
Network-dependent: peer discovery, official-source refresh, first WebLLM/model download.

stages.title: Safe update behavior
stages.body: Versioned service-worker caches remove old app-cache versions on activation while IndexedDB user records remain separate. A new deploy should not silently erase local work.
actions: Bump cache version on asset changes.
Keep schema migrations explicit.
Test repository subpath deployment on GitHub Pages.

stages.title: Operational PWA discipline
stages.body: Use deterministic precache lists, network/cache strategies by resource type, update messaging, quota-error handling and recovery paths. External CDN dependencies cannot be guaranteed offline by this same-origin service worker.
actions: Run Lighthouse/manual offline tests.
Verify all precache paths.
Keep an offline fallback page and export route.

title: Evidence & Provenance
summary: Keep official measurements, research, institutional analysis, preliminary data, scenarios and proposals visibly distinct.

stages.title: Every claim needs context
stages.body: A number without its source, date, geography and definition can mislead even when the number itself is accurate.
actions: Record source/publisher/date/geography.
Add evidence class A–F.
Write one limitation sentence.

stages.title: Separate evidence types
stages.body: Official administrative data, peer-reviewed findings, institutional analysis, preliminary releases, modeled scenarios and conceptual proposals answer different questions. Do not average them into one confidence score.
actions: Mark preliminary data clearly.
Keep current openings separate from projections.
Keep statewide shortage status separate from district vacancies.

stages.title: Track transformations
stages.body: Derived metrics should document formulas, exclusions, source versions and retrieval dates so another user can reproduce or challenge the result.
actions: Store raw-source references.
Expose scenario formulas.
Version superseded records rather than silently replacing history.

stages.title: Provenance as collaboration infrastructure
stages.body: In multidisciplinary work, provenance is how teams resolve disagreement without appealing to authority alone. Link decisions to evidence records, note dissent/uncertainty and preserve the record of what was known at the time.
actions: Attach evidence IDs to project decisions.
Require refresh dates for volatile sources.
Audit claims before public reporting.
